summary: Describes implementation strategies for two TCP mechanisms, the window and the acknowledgement, along with a set of algorithms tested in the field. This RFC is historic. Replaced by RFC 7805.

eli5.summary: TCP has to decide how much to send before waiting for a thank-you. This memo gives tried-and-true tips for doing that well.

subtitle: Tried-and-true algorithms for TCP window and acknowledgement handling.

tldr.problem: TCP implementations can produce very bad performance through inefficient window and acknowledgement strategies, even when complying with the specification.
tldr.mechanism: Provides tested algorithms for the sender and receiver to avoid Silly Window Syndrome (SWS) and optimize acknowledgement timing.
tldr.outcome: This RFC is Historic and has been replaced by RFC 7805 with more refined recommendations.

facts.label: CPU improvement observed
facts.value: Up to a factor of four

today: RFC 813 is Historic and has been replaced by RFC 7805, which provides updated and refined recommendations for window and acknowledgement strategies in TCP.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFC 813 describes implementation strategies for two core TCP mechanisms: the window (which controls how much data a sender can transmit) and the acknowledgement (which confirms receipt of data). While the TCP specification allows many valid implementations, some can suffer severe performance degradation. The RFC documents algorithms that have been tested in practice and work well together.
sections.eli5: TCP uses a window to control data flow and acknowledgements to say thank you. This memo explains the best way to do both without creating performance problems.

sections.title: The Mechanisms
sections.content:
The acknowledgement mechanism is fundamental to TCP: when data arrives, the receiver must send back an acknowledgement naming the highest-numbered byte received. The specification provides only general guidance on how promptly to acknowledge or how much data to acknowledge in each separate message.

The window mechanism is a flow control tool. The receiver returns a window value indicating the buffer space it has available. The sender may transmit only up to this window size until receiving an updated window value. When the window is zero, the sender must occasionally probe the receiver to see if more space is available.

Poor window algorithms can cause extreme throughput degradation of several factors of ten. This phenomenon is known as Silly Window Syndrome (SWS).
sections.eli5: The window tells the sender how much data it can send at once, like a mailbox that fills up. The acknowledgement is the receiver saying 'I got it'. If you send too many tiny messages, everything slows down.

sections.title: Silly Window Syndrome
sections.content:
SWS occurs when the sender transmits many small segments instead of waiting to accumulate a larger send. The problem develops over time during long data transfers. The RFC provides a detailed example: if the receiver processes a small amount of data and returns the same offered window size, the sender's usable window (offered window minus outstanding data) becomes small. The sender then sends a small segment, and when that acknowledgement returns, the same pattern repeats, creating a cascade of tiny segments.

SWS can be trivial to avoid. Either the sender or receiver algorithm alone is sufficient to prevent it completely, and using both together provides an additional reduction in CPU consumption observed in practice to be as high as a factor of four.
sections.eli5: Silly Window Syndrome happens when you send a postcard, get room for another postcard, send another postcard, and this tiny pattern repeats forever. The network gets clogged with millions of tiny messages.

sections.title: Improved Algorithms
sections.content:
The receiver's window algorithm prevents SWS by artificially reducing the offered window when processing small amounts of data. When sufficient new data has been processed, the receiver advertises the entire available space at once rather than small increments. A rule of thumb is to artificially reduce the offered window until the reduction constitutes at least one-half of available space, then open the window fully to advertise everything again.

The sender's algorithm is simpler: compute the usable window, and compare it to the offered window. If the ratio of usable to offered is less than a certain fraction (about 25 percent), refrain from sending. This requires adding only one line of code to most TCP implementations and works even when talking to implementations without SWS suppression.

The improved acknowledgement algorithm at the receiver avoids sending an acknowledgement unless one of three conditions holds: (1) the push bit is set in the incoming segment, (2) a revised window must be sent, or (3) a timeout occurs. This substantially reduces unnecessary acknowledgement traffic.
sections.eli5: The receiver holds back saying thank you until it has a lot to send or a big pause happens. The sender waits to accumulate more data before transmitting. Together these tricks prevent the tiny-postcard problem.

sections.title: Window Strategies
sections.content:
A conservative window strategy means the offered window reflects precisely the available buffer space. This approach limits throughput to one bufferfull per roundtrip delay, which can be problematic on high-delay networks.

An optimistic window strategy allows the offered window to exceed actual available buffer, gambling that the receiver can process incoming data faster than the sender transmits it. This works well when the receiver is faster than the sender but requires careful detection of lost segments when it fails.

The RFC also discusses sophisticated strategies for extreme-delay networks, such as spacing window openings over time to control the burstiness of arriving data. Such approaches have not been widely implemented, as most networks do not have sufficient delay to require them.
sections.eli5: Some networks are slow and far away, so you have to be clever about how big a window to advertise. A careful balance between conservative and aggressive strategies gives the best results.
